The manipulation of time in the story is very effective and well-balanced. The narrative stretches out two specific afternoons—one in June and one in July—using detailed dialogue, sensory descriptions, and small domestic actions (eating toast, pulling weeds, going to the hardware store) to establish the mother’s fiercely independent personality and the subtle signs of her aging. In contrast, the author compresses the dramatic medical event that happens in between (a month passing, the mother suffering heatstroke, ten days in the hospital, and a week in rehab) into just two brief paragraphs. This compression is entirely appropriate because the heart of the story is not the medical drama itself, but the quiet, poignant shift in the mother-child dynamic and the gradual erosion of the mother's memory and autonomy, which is best shown by contrasting the two unhurried visits.
